Case flow through a court: clearance, backlog and time to clear

Source: R/justice.R
case_flow.Rd

Turns the counts a court publishes each period – cases received, cases disposed and, when it is published, cases pending – into the measures used to judge whether a court is keeping up: the clearance rate (cases disposed per case received), its rolling value over a window, the net flow into the inventory and, with the pending count, the number of periods the current inventory would take to clear at the recent pace of disposition.

Usage

case_flow(
  received,
  disposed,
  pending = NULL,
  period = NULL,
  window = 12L,
  conf_level = 0.95
)

Arguments

received

Cases received (new cases), one per period, in time order.

disposed

Cases disposed, one per period.

pending

Optional cases pending at the end of each period.

period

Optional period labels: numbers, dates, or "YYYY-MM" strings (which the plot draws on a date axis).

window

Periods in the rolling clearance rate and in the pace behind periods_to_clear. Default 12, a year of months.

conf_level

Confidence level for the intervals. Default 0.95.

Value

A data frame of class rmbl_case_flow, one row per period: period, received, disposed, clearance with lower and upper, net (received less disposed: positive grows the inventory), rolling_clearance with rolling_lower and rolling_upper (NA until a full window is available), and either pending, pending_change and periods_to_clear, or, without pending, cumulative_net (the inventory change since the first period).

Details

A clearance rate above 1 means the court disposed of more cases than it received, so its inventory fell. The interval treats received and disposed as Poisson counts over the same period: given their sum, the disposed count is binomial, and the exact (Clopper-Pearson) limits for that proportion give exact limits for the ratio. The interval measures the period-to-period noise of counts this size; it does not make received and disposed the same cases, which they are not (a case disposed this month was usually received months before).

periods_to_clear divides the pending inventory by the mean number disposed over the last window periods (fewer at the start of the series). The published pending count need not equal the previous count plus the net flow – courts reactivate cases on bench warrants and transfer them – so pending_change is reported next to net rather than derived from it.

The result carries attribute "case_flow": window, conf_level and the totals received and disposed. Errors: received empty; a count vector that is not numeric, has a missing, negative or infinite value, or a length other than received's; period of another length, with missing or repeated values; window not a whole number of at least 1; conf_level outside (0, 1).

References

Ostrom, B. J. and Hanson, R. A. (1999). Efficiency, Timeliness, and Quality: A New Perspective from Nine State Criminal Trial Courts. National Center for State Courts, Williamsburg, VA. (Clearance rate and time-to-disposition measures.)

Ulm, K. (1990). A simple method to calculate the confidence interval of a standardized mortality ratio. American Journal of Epidemiology, 131(2), 373-375. (Exact limits for a ratio of Poisson counts through the beta distribution.)

See also

life_table, disposition_mix, stock_flow for custody populations.

Examples

f <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "ocj_flow_ontario.csv",
                          package = "rmoriebricklayer"))
cf <- case_flow(f$received, f$disposed, pending = f$pending, period = f$month)
cf

# without the pending count, a quarterly rolling window and 90% intervals
cq <- case_flow(f$received, f$disposed, period = f$month, window = 3, conf_level = 0.90)
head(as.data.frame(cq)[, c("period", "clearance", "rolling_clearance", "cumulative_net")])
